about: Plain-language explanations shown when the CHW types '?' (question plus options listed here) or '?N' (one option). Written as drafts by an AI assistant (Claude). An entry shows as 'Draft - not checked yet' until a teammate who checked it writes their name in checked_by.

Right Hypochondrium.text: The upper right part of the belly, just below the right ribs.

Epigastric.text: The upper middle part of the belly, just below where the ribs meet.

Left Hypochondrium.text: The upper left part of the belly, just below the left ribs.

Right Lumbar.text: The right side of the belly, at the level of the belly button.

Umbilical.text: The middle of the belly, around the belly button.

Left Lumbar.text: The left side of the belly, at the level of the belly button.

Right Iliac Fossa.text: The lower right part of the belly, just above the right hip bone.

Hypogastric/Suprapubic.text: The lower middle part of the belly, below the belly button and just above the private parts.

Left Iliac Fossa.text: The lower left part of the belly, just above the left hip bone.

Right scapula.text: The right shoulder blade, the flat bone on the upper back.

Groin.text: The fold where the top of the leg meets the lower belly.

Sacral region.text: The lowest part of the back, just above the buttocks.

Flanks.text: The sides of the body between the lowest ribs and the hips, toward the back.

Gradual.text: Came on slowly, little by little.

Rapidly increasing.text: Got worse quickly over a short time.

Sudden.text: Started all at once, without warning.

Constant.text: There all the time, without stopping.

Colicky / Intermittent (comes & goes).text: Pain that comes in waves: it gets strong, eases, and then comes back.

Gnawing/chewing.text: A nagging pain that feels like something is biting or chewing inside.

Cramping.text: A squeezing, tightening pain, like a muscle cramp.

Dull, aching.text: A steady, heavy pain that is not sharp.

Stabbing.text: A sudden sharp pain, like being poked with a knife.

Bloating.text: The belly feels full, tight, or swollen.

Static (Not change).text: Stays the same; not getting better or worse.

Continous.text: There all the time, without stopping.

Nausea.text: Feeling like you are going to vomit (throw up).

Vomiting.text: Throwing up food or liquid from the stomach through the mouth.

Anorexia.text: Not wanting to eat; not feeling hungry.

Diarrhea.text: Passing loose, watery stools (poop) more often than usual.

Constipation.text: Passing hard stools (poop), or passing stool less often than usual, often with pushing.

Fever.text: The body is hotter than normal.

Abdominal distention/Bloating.text: The belly feels full, tight, or swollen, or looks bigger than usual.

Belching/Burping.text: Air coming up from the stomach and out through the mouth.

Passing gas.text: Air coming out from the bottom (farting).

Change in appetite.text: Wanting to eat more or less than usual.

Color change in stool [describe].text: The stool (poop) is a different color than usual, for example black, red, or very pale.

Blood in stool.text: Blood in or on the stool (poop); it can look red, or make the stool black.

Change in frequency of urination [descri.text: Passing urine (peeing) more often or less often than usual.

Color change in urine [describe].text: The urine (pee) is a different color than usual, for example very dark, red, or brown.

Hiccups.text: Sudden jumps in the chest that make a 'hic' sound.

Restlessness.text: Not able to stay still or relax.

Injury.text: Being hurt, for example by a fall, a hit, or an accident.

Breathlessness.text: Feeling short of breath, or not able to get enough air.

Vaginal discharge [describe].text: Fluid or mucus that comes out of the vagina.

Curd-like.text: Thick and white, with lumps like curd (yogurt).

Medications [describe].text: A medicine; type which medicine made the pain less.

Pressure.text: Pushing or pressing on the painful area.

Straining.text: Pushing hard, for example when passing stool (poop) or lifting something heavy.

Leaning forward.text: Bending the upper body forward while sitting or standing.

Squatting.text: Sitting low on the feet with the knees fully bent.

Has not started menstruation.text: Has not had her first monthly period yet.

Menopause.text: Her monthly periods have stopped for good, usually around age 45 to 55.

Chills.text: Feeling very cold and shivering, often with a fever.

Loss of smell/taste sensation.text: Not able to smell things or taste food like before.

Loss of smell.text: Not able to smell things like before.

Loss of taste sensation.text: Not able to taste food like before.

Dry.text: A cough that brings up no mucus (phlegm).

Productive (With sputum).text: A cough that brings up mucus (phlegm) from the chest.

Wet.text: A cough that brings up mucus (phlegm).

Chest pain/discomfort.text: Pain or an uncomfortable feeling in the chest.

Joint pain.text: Pain where two bones meet, like the knee, elbow, wrist, or fingers.

General weakness.text: Feeling tired and weak all over the body.

Night sweats.text: Sweating a lot during sleep, enough to wet clothes or bedsheets.

Neck stiffness.text: The neck feels stiff and hurts when bending the head forward.

Burning sensation during urination.text: A burning or stinging feeling while passing urine (peeing).

Trouble when starting to urinate or trou.text: Hard to start peeing, or the stream of pee is weak or stops and starts.

Skin rash.text: Red spots, bumps, or patches on the skin.

Photosensitivity.text: Being bothered by light, for example bright light hurts the eyes or sunlight causes a rash on the skin.

Chronic liver disease.text: A long-lasting illness of the liver, the organ under the right ribs that cleans the blood.

Chronic renal disease.text: A long-lasting illness of the kidneys, the organs that clean the blood and make urine (pee).

HIV/AIDS.text: HIV is a virus that weakens the body's protection against infections, and AIDS is the late, serious stage of HIV.

All day/ Constant.text: The fever is there all day and does not go away.

Irregular (comes & goes).text: The fever comes and goes, with no fixed pattern.

Alternate days.text: The fever comes every other day: one day fever, the next day none.

Body Temperature (F).text: The temperature on the thermometer, in degrees Fahrenheit (normal is about 98.6 F).

Recent contact with persons having fever.text: Was recently close to someone who had a fever.

Recent travel.text: The patient or their family went on a trip recently.

Needles use (for drug).text: A needle was put into the body recently, for example to inject drugs.

Relapse.text: The same fever came back again after it had gone away.

Combined high and low.text: The fever is sometimes high and sometimes low.

Acute (0-2 weeks).text: Started recently: less than 2 weeks ago.

Chronic (More than 8 weeks).text: Has lasted a long time: more than 8 weeks (about 2 months).

Seasonal.text: Happens in a certain season of the year, like winter or the rainy season.

Wheezing.text: A high whistling sound when breathing, usually when breathing out.

Shortness of breath.text: Feeling like you cannot get enough air.

Pain/Tightness of chest.text: Pain in the chest, or a feeling that the chest is being squeezed.

Hemoptysis.text: Coughing up blood, or mucus (phlegm) with blood in it.

Weight change (kg).text: The patient's body weight has gone up or down.

Hoarseness.text: The voice sounds rough, croaky, or weak.

Burning feeling in a throat at night/ear.text: A hot, burning feeling in the throat at night or early in the morning, sometimes with a sour taste.

Nasal congestion/Stuffy nose.text: The nose feels blocked, so it is hard to breathe through it.

Runny nose.text: Liquid keeps coming out of the nose.

Post nasal drip.text: Mucus from the nose runs down the back of the throat, so the patient often needs to clear the throat or swallow.

Exposure to dusts/fumes.text: Breathing in dust, smoke, or chemical fumes, for example at work.

Recent severe stress.text: Feeling very worried, upset, or under a lot of pressure lately.

Recurrent diarrhoea.text: Loose, watery stools (poop) that keep coming back again and again.

Ex-smoker.text: Used to smoke but has stopped.

Declined to answer.text: The patient did not want to answer this question.

Incomplete.text: Some vaccines for the child's age are still missing.

Complete.text: All vaccines for the child's age have been given.

On-going.text: The child is still getting vaccines on schedule.

High Blood Pressure.text: The blood pushes too hard against the walls of the blood vessels; it often causes no symptoms.

Heart Problems.text: Any illness of the heart, such as a heart attack or a weak heart.

Stroke.text: Blood stops flowing to part of the brain, which can suddenly cause weakness on one side of the body, a drooping face, or trouble speaking.

Diabetes.text: A long-lasting illness where there is too much sugar in the blood.

Asthma.text: A long-lasting illness where the airways in the chest get tight, causing wheezing, coughing, and trouble breathing.

Tuberculosis.text: An infection, usually of the lungs, that causes a long-lasting cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss, and spreads through the air.

Cancer/Tumour.text: A lump or growth in the body that should not be there; cancer can spread and harm the body.

Operation.text: Surgery: a doctor cuts the body open to treat a problem.

Hospitalization.text: Staying in a hospital, usually overnight or longer, for treatment.

Surgery.text: An operation, where a doctor cuts the body open to fix a problem.

Angioplasty.text: A treatment where a doctor opens a blocked blood vessel of the heart using a thin tube with a tiny balloon.

Abdomen (Stomach/Liver/Bile/Kidney/Colon.text: The belly, including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, kidneys, and large bowel.

Prostate.text: A small gland in men, just below the bladder, that helps make semen.

C-Section.text: Delivering a baby through an operation that cuts through the belly and the womb.

Hysterectomy.text: An operation to remove the womb (uterus).

I always take them as prescribed.text: Always takes the medicine exactly as the doctor or health worker said.

Sometimes I take them as prescribed.text: Only sometimes takes the medicine the way the doctor or health worker said.

I seldom take them as prescribed.text: Rarely takes the medicine the way the doctor or health worker said.

Denied answer.text: The patient did not want to answer this question.

Denied.text: The patient did not want to answer this question.

High BP.text: High blood pressure: the blood pushes too hard against the walls of the blood vessels.

Heart Disease.text: Any illness of the heart, such as a heart attack or a weak heart.

Jaundice.text: The skin and the white part of the eyes turn yellow, often because of a liver problem.

Cancer.text: An illness where some cells in the body grow out of control and can spread.

Abdominal distention.text: The belly is swollen or looks bigger than usual.

Abnormal Bleeding.text: Bleeding that is not normal, for example very heavy, without a clear reason, or from an unusual place.

Blood in stool or Black stool.text: Blood in the stool (poop), which can look red, or make the stool black and sticky like tar.

Dizziness & Vertigo.text: Feeling light-headed or unsteady; vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning.

Dyspepsia.text: Indigestion: pain, burning, or a too-full feeling in the upper belly, usually after eating.

Fatigue & General weakness.text: Feeling very tired and weak most of the time.

Fever & Rash.text: Fever together with red spots, bumps, or patches on the skin.

Gait & balance disorder.text: Trouble walking normally or keeping balance.

Genital disease (Female).text: Problems of a woman's private parts, such as discharge, itching, sores, or pain.

Disorders of Hearing.text: Problems with hearing, such as hearing less or hearing ringing in the ears.

Hypertension follow up.text: A check-up visit for a patient who already has high blood pressure.

Hypertension screening.text: Checking a person's blood pressure to find out if it is too high.

Lymph node enlargement.text: Swollen glands: small lumps under the skin, often in the neck, armpit, or groin.

Muscle weakness or Paralysis.text: Muscles are weak, or a part of the body cannot move at all.

Numbness, Tingling, Sensory loss.text: Losing feeling in a part of the body, or a pins-and-needles feeling.

Oedema.text: Swelling caused by extra fluid in the body, often in the feet, legs, or face.

Oral Pain.text: Pain in the mouth, teeth, gums, or tongue.

Palpitations.text: Feeling the heart beat fast, hard, or unevenly.

Smell & Taste disorder.text: Problems with smelling or tasting, for example losing the sense of smell.

Syncope.text: Fainting: suddenly passing out for a short time and falling down.

Urine disturbance.text: Any problem with passing urine (pee), such as pain, burning, or going too often.

Vomiting Blood.text: Throwing up blood, which can look red or like coffee grounds.

Main complaint.text: Asks for the main health problem that made the patient come today.

Since when have you had this symptom?.text: Asks how long the patient has had this problem, for example 3 days or 2 weeks.

Do you have the following symptom(s)?.text: Asks if the patient has any of these other problems along with the main one.

Have you taken any treatment (including.text: Asks if the patient already took any medicine or home remedy, or saw anyone for help, for this problem.

Additional information.text: A place to write anything else important the patient said that was not asked above.

Other [describe].text: Type the patient's answer in their own words, because it is not in the list.

Yes [Describe].text: Type what the patient said, in a few words.

Describe.text: Type the patient's answer in a few words.

[Enter since when].text: Asks how long ago this started, for example 2 weeks or 5 years.

Since when.text: Asks how long ago this started, or the date it started.

Since.text: Asks how long ago this started, for example 5 years.

When.text: Asks the date when this happened.

on.text: Asks the date when this happened.

Which part of the abdomen do you feel pa.text: Asks where on the belly the pain is; the abdomen is the belly, between the chest and the hips.

Does the pain move to other parts of the.text: Asks if the pain stays in one place or also spreads to another part of the body, like the back or shoulder.

Pain radiates to.text: Asks where else the pain spreads to from where it started.

How did the pain start?.text: Asks if the pain came on slowly, got worse quickly, or started all at once.

What time of the day do you feel the pai.text: Asks if the pain is worse at a certain time of day, like in the morning or at night.

Character of the pain.text: Asks what the pain feels like, for example steady, coming and going, cramping, or a dull ache.

How severe is the pain?.text: Asks how bad the pain is, from 1 (a little pain) to 10 (the worst pain the patient can imagine).

Change in appetite.text: Asks if the patient wants to eat more or less than usual.

Color change in stool [describe].text: Type the new color of the stool (poop), for example black, red, or very pale.

Change in frequency of urination [descri.text: Type how the patient passes urine (pees) more often or less often than usual.

Color change in urine [describe].text: Type the new color of the urine (pee), for example very dark, red, or brown.

Is the discharge foul-smelling?.text: Asks if the fluid coming from the vagina has a bad smell.

Character of the discharge [describe].text: Asks what the fluid from the vagina looks like, for example thick and white, green, watery, or with blood.

What worsens the pain?.text: Asks what makes the pain worse, like eating, moving, or coughing.

What relieves/lessens the pain?.text: Asks what makes the pain better or less, like medicine, food, or sitting a certain way.

Medications [describe].text: Type the name of the medicine that makes the pain less.

Menstrual history.text: Asks about the patient's monthly periods: if they have started, are still coming, or have stopped for good.

Age at onset.text: Asks how old the patient was when her monthly periods first started.

Last menstruation period.text: Asks the date the patient's last monthly period started.

Age at menopause.text: Asks how old the patient was when her monthly periods stopped for good.

Nature of fever.text: Asks about the pattern of the fever: is it there all the time, or does it come and go?

In a day, when do you feel fever the mos.text: Asks at what time of day the fever is worst, like morning, evening, or night.

Severity.text: Asks how strong the fever is: low (body a little warm), moderate (in between), or high (body very hot).

Did you recently measure fever using the.text: Asks if the patient's body temperature was checked with a thermometer recently.

Body Temperature (F).text: Asks the number shown on the thermometer, in degrees Fahrenheit (normal is about 98.6 F).

Loss of smell/taste sensation.text: Asks if the patient lost their sense of smell, their sense of taste, or both.

Cough.text: Asks what kind of cough the patient has: dry, or bringing up mucus (phlegm).

Productive (With sputum).text: Asks about the mucus (phlegm) the patient coughs up.

Color of sputum.text: Asks the color of the mucus (phlegm) the patient coughs up.

Chest pain/discomfort.text: Asks more about the pain or uncomfortable feeling in the chest.

Site.text: Asks where exactly the pain or discomfort is.

While breathing in, do both sides of the.text: Asks if the bottom of the chest sinks inward each time the patient breathes in, which shows breathing is hard work.

Do you experience a grunting noise in ch.text: Asks if the patient makes a short, low 'uh' sound each time they breathe out.

Abdominal pain.text: Asks more about the pain in the belly.

How did the abdominal pain start?.text: Asks if the belly pain came on quickly or slowly.

How has the abdominal pain progressed?.text: Asks how the belly pain has changed over time: coming and going, staying the same, or getting worse.

Describe the pain.text: Asks what the pain feels like, for example steady, cramping, stabbing, or burning.

When does the pain increase?.text: Asks when the pain gets worse, for example before or after eating.

Does the pain go to other part of the bo.text: Asks if the pain spreads to another place, like the chest, neck, or back.

Joint pain.text: Asks more about the pain in the joints (the places where bones meet, like knees, elbows, and fingers).

Does the pain involve single or multiple.text: Asks if the pain is in one joint or in many joints (joints are where bones meet, like knees and elbows).

Single joint [Describe which joint].text: Type which joint hurts, for example right knee.

Multiple joints [Describe which joints].text: Type which joints hurt, for example both knees and wrists.

Pain in any other location.text: Asks where else in the body the patient has pain.

Have you ever been diagnosed with any of.text: Asks if a doctor or health worker ever told the patient they have one of these long-lasting illnesses.

Have you experienced the following situa.text: Asks about things that happened in the months before the fever began.

Any recent contact with any persons with.text: Asks if the patient was recently close to someone who had a fever.

Did you/your family travel recently?.text: Asks if the patient or their family went on a trip recently.

Where.text: Asks the place the patient or family travelled to.

Have you recently been hospitalized?.text: Asks if the patient recently stayed in a hospital.

Have you recently used any needles (eg:.text: Asks if a needle was recently put into the patient's body, for example to inject drugs.

Have you had this fever before as well?.text: Asks if the patient had the same kind of fever in the past.

Has there been a recent epidemic in the.text: Asks if many people in the village or area have recently become sick with the same illness.

Is there a specific time of occurence of.text: Asks if the cough happens more at a certain time or in a certain situation, like at night or when lying down.

Which season.text: Asks in which season of the year the cough happens, for example winter or the rainy season.

What aggravates the cough?.text: Asks what makes the cough worse.

Is the cough dry or wet?.text: Asks if the cough brings up mucus (phlegm): dry means no mucus, wet means mucus comes up.

What is the colour of the sputum?.text: Asks the color of the mucus (phlegm) the patient coughs up.

Weight change (kg).text: Asks how much the patient's body weight has gone up or down, in kilograms.

Weight gain.text: Asks how many kilograms the patient has gained.

Weight loss.text: Asks how many kilograms the patient has lost.

Have you taken any medication recently?.text: Asks if the patient has taken any medicine in the last few days or weeks.

Do you smoke/have ever smoked?.text: Asks if the patient smokes now or smoked in the past, for example cigarettes or bidis.

How many cigarettes per day did you smok.text: Asks how many cigarettes (or bidis) the patient smoked each day.

What is your occupation?.text: Asks what work the patient does, for example farming or construction.

Any exposure to dusts/fumes?.text: Asks if the patient breathes in dust, smoke, or chemical fumes, for example at work.

Yes.text: Fill in the details for the patient's 'Yes' answer.

Other.text: Type the other answer in the patient's own words.

Frequency.text: Asks how often the patient does this, for example how many times a day.

[Describe location of pain].text: Type where else in the body the patient has pain.

[Enter if known].text: Type the latest blood sugar and HbA1C numbers, if the patient knows them.

Has your child been vaccinated?.text: Asks if the child has had the vaccines (shots or drops that protect against diseases) for their age.

Pregnancy status.text: Asks if the patient is pregnant now.

Do you have a history of any of the foll.text: Asks if the patient has ever had any of these illnesses or events in the past.

Diagnosed on.text: Asks the date when a doctor or health worker first found this illness.

Current medication.text: Asks what medicines the patient takes now for this illness.

What was the problem?.text: Asks what the heart problem was, in the patient's words.

Occured/Diagnosed on.text: Asks the date it happened or when a doctor found it.

How was it treated?.text: Asks what treatment the patient got for it.

When were you diagnosed?.text: Asks the date when a doctor or health worker first found this illness.

Last measured Blood Sugar and HbA1C.text: Asks for the patient's most recent blood sugar test results; HbA1C is a blood test that shows the average sugar level over about 3 months.

Did you take treatment?.text: Asks if the patient took medicine for this illness.

How long did you take the treatment?.text: Asks for how many weeks or months the patient took the medicine.

Describe the disease.text: Asks what kind of cancer or growth the patient has and where in the body it is.

What was the operation?.text: Asks which part of the body was operated on.

Reason.text: Asks why the patient was in the hospital.

How long were you hospitalized?.text: Asks how many days or weeks the patient stayed in the hospital.

Have you recently taken any kind of medi.text: Asks if the patient took any medicine lately, including traditional or herbal medicines.

Name of Medications.text: Asks the names of the medicines the patient took.

Medication Name.text: Asks the name of the medicine.

From.text: Asks the date the patient started taking this medicine.

To.text: Asks the date the patient stopped taking this medicine.

How often do you have trouble taking med.text: Asks how often the patient misses doses or does not take medicines the way the doctor or health worker said.

Do you have any allergies?.text: Asks if any medicine, food, or other thing has ever caused a bad reaction, like a rash, swelling, or trouble breathing.

Do you chew tobbaco?.text: Asks if the patient chews tobacco, for example gutka, khaini, or paan with tobacco.

How often do you chew tobacco?.text: Asks how many times a day the patient chews tobacco.

Smoking history.text: Asks if the patient smokes now, smoked in the past, or never smoked.

How many cigarettes per day do you smoke.text: Asks how many cigarettes (or bidis) the patient smokes each day.

Alcohol use.text: Asks if the patient drinks alcohol, like beer, wine, or local liquor.

How often do you take alcohol?.text: Asks how often the patient drinks alcohol, for example every day or once a week.

No. of drinks consumed in one go.text: Asks how many drinks the patient has at one time.

Do you have a family history of any of t.text: Asks if a close family member (mother, father, sister, or brother) has had any of these illnesses.

[Describe relation].text: Type which other family member has it, for example grandmother or uncle.
